sections.html:
The county recorder page gives weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, or fax 740-439-6267. Cambridge is the county seat, and the auditor works from the Administration Building at 627 Wheeling Avenue.

Ohio recorders hold the ownership record for land and each lien against it. A seller whose own deed was never recorded should expect the buyer's title company to pause the sale until that gap is closed, so check your deed's recording stamp before you list.

sections.h2: Does Guernsey County take electronic deeds?
sections.html:
Yes. Four submitting vendors can send eRecordings to the recorder, a route used mostly by lenders, banks, attorneys and title companies. Only document types the office accepts by regular mail qualify, and each vendor sets its own price.

A second route, described on the auditor's page, is e-filing through Kofile Technologies. Files can be sent every hour of every day, but staff process them only between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays, so a late upload waits a business day. Plats and military discharges (DD-214) cannot go this way. When a deed or conveyance form is rejected, processing restarts once the corrected version arrives.

sections.h2: What happens at the auditor before recording
sections.html:
Real estate staff at the auditor move the deed onto the tax records and then pass it to the recorder. The office is in suite 301 at 627 Wheeling Avenue, and the phone is (740) 432-9243, option 1 for real estate. Forms for sellers and closing agents include:

  • DTE 100, the real estate conveyance form, and DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers
  • DTE 101, the statement of conveyance of homestead property
  • DTE 102, the statement of conveyance of CAUV property
  • A routing sheet and a timeline for deed transfers
  • Transfer and Conveyance Standards effective October 1, 2022

A conveyance fee calculator sits under tools on the auditor's site. State fees come from R.C. 319.54 ($1.00 per thousand) and R.C. 322.02 (a county transfer tax of up to 30 cents per hundred dollars), so use the calculator or call the auditor for the Guernsey County total.

R.C. 319.202 governs the form. The buyer or the buyer's representative files it before the auditor endorses the deed. It declares the property's value, meaning the whole price with any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and willfully falsifying that figure is prohibited.

The same statute adds questions on tax reductions and farm status:

  • Either an affirmation that the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's taxes, or a sworn statement giving the reduction and its estimated amount.
  • Either an affirmation about current agricultural use valuation (CAUV) status, or a sworn statement noting a possible recoupment charge.
  • The reason for any exemption, written on the form when no fee is due.

After endorsement the auditor retains the original, sends a copy to the tax commissioner and hands one to the buyer. Residential rental property gets an added notice telling the buyer to register with the auditor.

sections.h2: Recording fees at the Guernsey County Recorder
sections.html:
Charges follow R.C. 317.32. Combined, the Ohio Recorders' Association table reads $34.00 for the opening two pages, $8.00 per page after that and $4.00 per marginal notation, with up to $5.00 per document for preservation. Half of every fee funds basic recording and the other half the state's Housing Trust Fund.

The table also lists a $10.00 plus $10.00 standardization fee for a document that misses the formatting rules. Call the recorder at 740-432-9275 to ask whether Guernsey County adds the surcharge, because each county decides that for itself.

sections.h2: Who can notarize a deed signed in Guernsey County?
sections.html:
After the grantor signs, someone from the list in R.C. 5301.01 has to witness the acknowledgment. That list takes in notaries, mayors, the auditor, the engineer, and judges or court clerks. Banks, title companies and law offices usually keep a notary on staff.

R.C. 5301.25 sends each deed to the county where the land sits and treats an unrecorded one as fraudulent against a later buyer acting in good faith. A deed made after a survey must carry the surveyor's name.

The auditor's information page explains the homestead rules behind the statement questions above. A homeowner qualifies by owning and occupying the home as a principal residence on January 1 of the year of application, and by meeting one of three tests: age 65 by December 31 of the filing year, total and permanent disability, or being the surviving spouse of a past recipient who was at least 59. Owners with more than one home count as living where they are registered to vote and where their federal income tax form places them.

Ohio returned to income testing in 2013, but anyone who received the credit for tax year 2013 keeps it without an income limit. Owners with a qualifying federal disability rating from military service receive a reduction equal to the tax on $50,000 of true value, compared with $25,000 for the standard credit. The spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty receives the same $50,000 level with no income limit.

The auditor's delinquent tax notice cites R.C. 5721.03 and warns that listed parcels will be certified for foreclosure or a tax certificate sale unless every delinquent tax, assessment, interest and penalty is paid within a year. If your parcel is on that list, pay it at or before closing.

sections.h2: Owners and housing in Guernsey County
sections.html:
The auditor counts 40,170 parcels, and Census estimates give 38,379 residents in 2025, about level with 2020. Owners hold 72.1 percent of homes, with a $157,700 median in the 2020 to 2024 survey, while renters pay a $864 median gross rent. There are 16,318 households averaging 2.31 people, and 19,116 housing units as of 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,237 with a mortgage and $505 without one. Forty-one building permits were issued in 2025.

The auditor's forms list includes a Mineral Deeds section, so ask the buyer's title company to search for any recorded mineral deed or lease on the parcel.

sections.h2: Where Guernsey County deeds are recorded
sections.html:
Buffalo, Kimbolton and Salesville are census-designated places outside Cambridge, and deeds for land there are recorded in the same Cambridge office. The same is true for every township in the county.

In practice a sale here runs in order. The closing agent prepares the deed and the DTE form, the grantor signs before a notary, the auditor endorses and moves the deed on the tax records, and the recorder files it. The buyer's title company usually handles the trip, but a seller can ask for the recording date to confirm the deed is on file.

faqs.q: When is the Guernsey County Recorder open?
faqs.a: Weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, and note that electronic filings get processed only until 3 p.m.

faqs.q: Can a deed be eRecorded in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: Yes, through one of four submitting vendors or through Kofile e-filing. Plats and military discharges are excluded, and a title company usually handles the upload.

faqs.q: Does the deed go to the auditor or the recorder first?
faqs.a: The auditor, who transfers it on the tax records with a conveyance form and then forwards it to the recorder. The auditor posts a timeline for deed transfers.

faqs.q: What is the basic recording charge in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: The Ohio Recorders' Association table shows $34.00 for two pages plus $8.00 for each added page, and up to $5.00 as a preservation surcharge. Ask the recorder about any county surcharge.

faqs.q: What is the risk of leaving a deed unrecorded?
faqs.a: R.C. 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later buyer who acted in good faith without notice. Record it as soon as the auditor has transferred it.
